level.algeria_1830.fact: The blow of the fly whisk was only a pretext. In May 1830 a fleet carried General de Bourmont's 37,000 soldiers to Algiers. On June 14 they landed at Sidi Ferruch, routed the dey's army at Staouéli, and on July 5 Hussein Dey signed the capitulation and left for exile in Naples. The treasury of the regency fell to France. Three weeks later the July Revolution toppled Charles X, but the new government kept Algeria. In 1832 the western tribes chose as their emir the 24-year-old Abd al-Qadir, son of a Sufi sheikh. He built a state of his own, with an army, taxes and capitals, signed treaties with France — in 1837 General Bugeaud himself signed the Treaty of Tafna — and went to war again. Bugeaud, by then governor-general, answered with "scorched earth": flying columns burned crops and orchards and drove off the livestock; in the caves of Dahra in 1845, Pélissier's soldiers suffocated hundreds of people sheltering inside with smoke. In 1847 Abd al-Qadir surrendered on condition he could leave for the East, yet he was held prisoner in France for five years. The conquest and colonization of Algeria dragged on for decades and cost the lives of hundreds of thousands of Algerians.
level.algeria_1830.goal: For the sake of prestige, the king takes Algiers — but taking a city is not taking a country: the tribes choose Abd al-Qadir as their emir
level.algeria_1830.hint: The fly whisk is only the pretext, not the cause. The city falls in three weeks, the country takes decades. In the 1830s this story is far from over.
level.algeria_1830.intro: 1827. Algiers is a semi-independent regency of the Ottoman Empire. France has long owed Algerian merchants for grain supplied to its army back in the days of the Directory. In a quarrel over this debt, Hussein Dey struck the French consul Pierre Deval with a fly whisk. For three years France has kept up a blockade, and the unpopular Charles X needs a resounding victory.
level.algeria_1830.source: Capitulation of Algiers (July 5, 1830); Treaty of Tafna (1837); Alexis de Tocqueville, 'Travail sur l'Algérie' (1841)
level.algeria_1830.title: Algeria: Landing and Resistance
level.beziers_1209.fact: Trencavel tried to submit to the legate but was turned away, and he rode off to prepare Carcassonne for defense. On July 22, 1209, Bishop Renaud de Montpeyroux of Béziers brought the townspeople a list of some two hundred and twenty suspected heretics and urged them to hand them over — the city refused. While the knights were still deliberating, the camp followers, the "ribauds," burst through the gates; people were slaughtered even inside the churches, and the city was burned. The legates wrote to the pope of twenty thousand dead — a figure that was evidently much exaggerated. The famous line "Kill them all, God will know His own" was written down some ten years later by the German monk Caesarius of Heisterbach, and most historians doubt that Arnaud Amalric ever said it. In August Trencavel came to parley outside Carcassonne, was seized, and died in prison in November; his lands went to Simon IV de Montfort — father of the English rebel Simon de Montfort. The war lasted twenty years: northern barons took lands in the south, and Languedoc passed into the royal domain. The Inquisition hunted the Cathars; Montségur, one of their chief refuges, fell in 1244, and Quéribus, which fell in 1255, is usually named as the last stronghold linked to the Cathars.
level.beziers_1209.goal: Crusaders against the Cathars: Béziers, which refused to give up its heretics, is massacred, Viscount Trencavel is seized at a parley, and his lands go to Simon de Montfort
level.beziers_1209.hint: The legate is not looking for peace. Whoever stays in Béziers will never see Carcassonne — and it is those still holding out who get invited to the parley tent.
level.beziers_1209.intro: Summer 1209. In the south, in Languedoc, many townspeople and nobles sympathize with the Cathars — the "good men" whom Rome considers heretics. Pope Innocent III has proclaimed a crusade against them, and a huge army is marching from the north under the legate Arnaud Amalric, abbot of Cîteaux. The lands of Béziers and Carcassonne belong to the 24-year-old Viscount Raymond-Roger Trencavel.
level.beziers_1209.source: Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, 'Historia Albigensis'; 'Canso de la Crotzada'; Caesarius of Heisterbach, 'Dialogus miraculorum'
level.beziers_1209.title: Béziers
level.capet_987.fact: The archbishop's trial was convened at Senlis with Hugh presiding — and the charges were dropped. At the same assembly, according to the chronicler Richer of Reims, Adalbero declared: "The throne is not acquired by hereditary right" — and proposed Hugh, rejecting Charles as one who served a foreign king. In the summer of 987 Hugh was anointed king — at Noyon, or by other accounts at Reims. The archbishop's speeches and letters were written by the scholar Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II. The power of the first Capetians was weak: many dukes and counts were richer than the king. To keep the crown in the family, Hugh had his son Robert crowned co-ruler as early as December 987. In 991 Charles of Lorraine was betrayed to Hugh by the Bishop of Laon. The direct Capetians ruled until 1328, and their cadet branches — the Valois and the Bourbons — until 1848.
level.capet_987.goal: The last Carolingian on the West Frankish throne has died childless — the Archbishop of Reims persuades the nobles that the crown goes by merit, not blood, and crowns Hugh Capet
level.capet_987.hint: A man accused of treason cannot lead the assembly — the trial comes first. And whoever has sworn to the Carolingian bloodline will never put Capet forward.
level.capet_987.intro: May 987. The young King Louis V, the last Carolingian on the throne of the West Franks, has died in a hunting accident, leaving no son. Before his death he was about to try Archbishop Adalbero of Reims for treason. The dead king's uncle, Charles of Lorraine, has a claim to the crown — but he is a vassal of the German king. The most powerful lord in the land is Hugh, Duke of the Franks, nicknamed Capet.
level.capet_987.source: Richer of Reims, 'Historiae' (c. 991–998); letters of Gerbert of Aurillac
level.capet_987.title: The Choice of Hugh Capet
level.castillon_1453.fact: Bureau ringed his camp with a ditch and an earthen rampart and placed a mass of cannon behind it — by various estimates, up to three hundred guns of different calibers. On July 17 Talbot was told that dust was rising over the camp and the French were leaving — in fact it was the camp servants leading the horses away. Talbot attacked with whatever troops had arrived, without waiting for the rest of his infantry. By tradition he wore no armor: once released from captivity, he had sworn never again to wear it against the King of France. The English columns ran into point-blank fire; a cannonball killed Talbot's horse, and the earl himself was finished off with an axe. On October 19 Bordeaux surrendered. No peace treaty was ever signed, but the Hundred Years' War ended there: on the continent England was left with only Calais — until 1558. Yet English monarchs bore the title "King of France" until 1801.
level.castillon_1453.goal: Believing the French are fleeing, Talbot attacks Jean Bureau's fortified camp — and cannon decide the last battle of the Hundred Years' War
level.castillon_1453.hint: In open field the English are still strong — let them attack the rampart. And a cautious commander won't attack: he needs news that the enemy is running.
level.castillon_1453.intro: July 1453, Guyenne. Nearly all of England's possessions in France are already lost, but the people of Bordeaux, who have traded wine with England for three hundred years, have called the English back. The old commander John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury — past sixty-five — has retaken the city. The French army is besieging Castillon on the Dordogne, and its artillery is commanded by Jean Bureau.
level.castillon_1453.source: Mathieu d'Escouchy, 'Chronique'; Thomas Basin, 'Histoire de Charles VII'
level.castillon_1453.title: Castillon
level.charlemagne_800.fact: Charles escorted the pope back to Rome with honor and in December 800 came there himself. Leo's enemies accused him of crimes, but no one dared to judge the pope: "the first see is judged by no one." On December 23 Leo publicly swore on the Gospels that he was innocent. And on December 25, during Christmas Mass at St. Peter's, he set a crown on Charles's head, and the Romans shouted three times: "To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, life and victory!" Einhard claims Charles said that had he known beforehand, he would never have entered the church — historians debate whether this was modesty or displeasure that the crown came from the pope. The Byzantine chronicler Theophanes writes that Charles later even sought Irene's hand. Constantinople recognized Charles's title only in 812. Charlemagne's empire is the shared history of future France, Germany and Italy, not the "first French empire."
level.charlemagne_800.goal: Driven out by the Romans, the pope seeks Charles's protection, clears himself by oath — and at Christmas 800 crowns the King of the Franks emperor
level.charlemagne_800.hint: He who crowns must himself be clean — but not by the king's verdict. Let Constantinople stay on the sidelines.
level.charlemagne_800.intro: 799. In Rome, noble relatives of the previous pope attack Leo III in the middle of a procession and try to blind him and cut out his tongue. Leo flees across the Alps to Paderborn, to the most powerful ruler in the West — Charles, King of the Franks. In Constantinople, meanwhile, Empress Irene reigns — the first woman on the throne of the Romans — and in the West many believe the imperial throne is effectively vacant.
level.charlemagne_800.source: Einhard, 'Vita Karoli Magni', ch. 28; 'Annales regni Francorum' for 799–801; 'Liber Pontificalis' (Life of Leo III)
level.charlemagne_800.title: A Crown in Rome
level.civil_code_1804.fact: The commission wrote the draft in four months. In the Council of State Bonaparte chaired about half of more than a hundred sessions and argued over every section. In 1801–1802 the Tribunate, where Benjamin Constant spoke, rejected the first titles; Bonaparte withdrew the bill and purged the opposition tribunes. On March 21, 1804, 36 laws were combined into the "Civil Code of the French" of 2,281 articles. It enshrined civil equality among men, civil marriage, freedom of property and contract, and equal division of inheritance among children — the end of primogeniture. But Article 213 read: "The husband owes protection to his wife, the wife owes obedience to her husband"; a married woman could not manage property without her husband. Bonaparte kept divorce, though he restricted it. Slavery in the colonies, restored in 1802, the Code left untouched. The "Napoleonic Code" spread across Europe and Latin America; on St. Helena Napoleon himself said the Code would outlive his victories.
level.civil_code_1804.goal: Lawyers merge the laws of three hundred provincial customs into one code, and Bonaparte pushes it through — with equality of men before the law and a husband's power over his wife
level.civil_code_1804.hint: First the draft, then the debate, then the law. The tribunes will bury it — don't give them the floor too early.
level.civil_code_1804.intro: 1800. France has some three hundred local bodies of customary law: Roman law in the south, the coutumes in the north — and on top of them, ten years of revolutionary legislation. First Consul Bonaparte charges four jurists — Portalis, Tronchet, Bigot de Préameneu and Maleville — with writing a single civil code.
level.civil_code_1804.source: Code civil des Français (March 21, 1804); J.-É. Portalis, 'Discours préliminaire sur le projet de Code civil' (1801)
level.civil_code_1804.title: The Civil Code
level.clermont_1095.fact: On November 27, 1095, Urban II called on the faithful to help the Eastern Christians and free Jerusalem, promising participants remission of sins; the text of the speech has not survived — we know it from retellings by Fulcher of Chartres, Robert the Monk and others, written down after 1099. According to Robert the Monk, the crowd shouted "God wills it!" The first to take the cross was Bishop Adhemar of Le Puy, and the pope made him legate of the expedition; Count Raymond IV of Toulouse announced through envoys that he would go. The pope set the departure for August 15, 1096. But crowds of the poor following the preacher Peter the Hermit set out earlier, and nearly all perished at the hands of the Turks near Civetot. In the spring of 1096, the bands of Count Emicho carried out pogroms against the Jews of Speyer, Worms and Mainz. The princes' armies took Jerusalem in 1099 and massacred Muslims and Jews in the city. Adhemar did not live to see it — he died of illness at Antioch in 1098.
level.clermont_1095.goal: At Clermont, Pope Urban II calls for a march on Jerusalem: Bishop Adhemar becomes legate, and the Count of Toulouse leads his army out on the appointed date
level.clermont_1095.hint: First the sermon, then the princes' vows. Whoever leaves early with the crowd will never reach Jerusalem.
level.clermont_1095.intro: November 1095, Clermont in Auvergne. The Byzantine emperor is asking the West for help against the Seljuk Turks, and Pope Urban II, a Frenchman from Champagne, wants to reconcile knights who fight one another endlessly and to raise Rome's authority. In a field outside the city, thousands await him — bishops, knights, common people.
level.clermont_1095.source: Fulcher of Chartres, 'Historia Hierosolymitana'; Robert the Monk, 'Historia Hierosolymitana'
level.clermont_1095.title: The Call at Clermont
level.clovis_496.fact: Gregory of Tours relates that in battle against the Alamanni, Clovis in despair called on "Clotilde's God" and won, and afterwards was baptized at Reims. Bishop Remigius greeted him with the words: "Bow your head meekly, Sicambrian: worship what you have burned, and burn what you have worshipped." Three thousand warriors were baptized with the king. Historians debate the date — anywhere from 496 to 508. Choosing Catholicism rather than Arianism made Clovis one of their own for the Gallo-Roman bishops and cities. In 507 he marched against the Arian Visigoths, saying it grieved him to see heretics holding part of Gaul. At Vouillé near Poitiers the Franks won, Clovis killed Alaric II with his own hand, and Aquitaine up to the Pyrenees passed to the Franks. The baptism of Clovis was not the "birth of France," but it was an important step toward the alliance of Frankish power and the Church.
level.clovis_496.goal: The King of the Franks is baptized in the Catholic rite, wins the support of the bishops of Gaul — and takes Aquitaine from the Visigoths
level.clovis_496.hint: Faith picks your allies: Gaul will not trust an Arian. And better not march on the Visigoths without the bishops.
level.clovis_496.intro: The end of the 5th century. Clovis rules the Franks and is still a pagan. His wife, the Burgundian princess Clotilde, is a Catholic and keeps urging her husband to be baptized. But Germanic kings have their own fashion: the Visigoths and Burgundians are Arian Christians, while most Gallo-Romans and their bishops are Catholics, to whom Arianism is heresy.
level.clovis_496.title: The Baptism of Clovis
level.commune_1871.fact: On the morning of March 18 soldiers came for the cannons, but townspeople — among them the schoolteacher Louise Michel — and National Guardsmen surrounded them, and the soldiers refused to fire. The crowd shot Generals Lecomte and Clément-Thomas. Thiers withdrew the government to Versailles. On March 26 Paris elected the Commune: it included workers like the bookbinder Eugène Varlin and journalists like Jules Vallès. The Commune separated church and state, abolished night work for bakers, handed abandoned workshops to the workers — and took hostages of its own. On May 21 the Versailles army entered the city. During the Bloody Week, by various estimates, seven to twenty thousand Parisians died, many shot without trial. In response the Communards killed hostages, among them the Archbishop of Paris, and set fire to the Tuileries and the Hôtel de Ville. Varlin was captured and shot on May 28. Louise Michel was deported to New Caledonia; Vallès fled to London. Amnesty came only in 1880. Some remember the Commune as the first workers' government, others as a revolt in a defeated country.
level.commune_1871.goal: Thiers tries to seize the cannons, Paris rises and elects the Commune, and two months later the Versailles army takes the city in the Bloody Week
level.commune_1871.hint: The uprising begins over the cannons, not the elections. Vallès will go into exile — don't put him in the line of fire in the last week.
level.commune_1871.intro: March 1871. The war is lost, Paris has endured siege and famine, and a new assembly with a monarchist majority sits at Versailles. The head of the executive, Adolphe Thiers, decides to disarm the capital: on Montmartre stand cannons bought with the Parisians' own money for the National Guard.
level.commune_1871.source: Louise Michel, 'La Commune' (1898); Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray, 'Histoire de la Commune de 1871' (1876)
level.commune_1871.title: The Paris Commune
level.compiegne_1918.fact: Clemenceau became prime minister on November 16, 1917, and in March 1918 declared in the Chamber: "Domestic policy? I wage war. Foreign policy? I wage war." He put politicians suspected of "defeatism" on trial and toured the trenches. In the spring of 1918 the Germans broke through the front, and on March 26 at Doullens the Allies entrusted Ferdinand Foch with coordination, and soon with supreme command. In the summer Foch went on the offensive. The American president Woodrow Wilson proposed peace on the basis of the "Fourteen Points"; Clemenceau reportedly smirked: "Even the good Lord had only ten." The armistice terms made continuing the war impossible: evacuate Belgium, France and Alsace-Lorraine within 15 days, withdraw from the left bank of the Rhine, which the Allies would occupy, hand over five thousand guns, intern the main surface warships and surrender the submarines. On November 11, 1918, at about a quarter past five in the morning, in Foch's railway carriage at Rethondes in the Forest of Compiègne, Matthias Erzberger signed them; at 11 o'clock the guns fell silent. Clemenceau was dubbed "Père la Victoire," the Father of Victory. Its price was some 1.4 million French dead. Alsace and Lorraine returned to France, and the peace itself was signed at Versailles in 1919.
level.compiegne_1918.goal: Clemenceau takes power with a single slogan, "I wage war," Foch gets unified command — and in a railway carriage near Compiègne Germany signs the armistice
level.compiegne_1918.hint: First unified command, then the terms. A peace "without victors" won't satisfy the Tiger.
level.compiegne_1918.intro: November 1917. France is exhausted: over a million soldiers have died in three years, the army has barely survived mutinies, and in Paris people talk of peace at any price. President Poincaré, though he dislikes him, calls on the 76-year-old Georges Clemenceau, nicknamed the Tiger, to become prime minister.
level.compiegne_1918.source: Armistice terms of November 11, 1918; Georges Clemenceau, 'Grandeurs et misères d'une victoire' (1930)
level.compiegne_1918.title: Father of Victory
level.coup_1851.fact: On the night of December 2, 1851 — the anniversary of Austerlitz and of Napoleon I's coronation — troops occupied Paris, and opposition leaders were arrested in their beds. A decree posted on the walls dissolved the Assembly and… restored universal male suffrage: Louis-Napoléon cast himself as the people's champion against the deputies. On December 3 Deputy Alphonse Baudin climbed a barricade in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine; workers refused to defend "deputies on 25 francs a day," and Baudin replied: "You will see how a man dies for 25 francs" — and was killed. On December 4 troops fired into the crowd on the boulevards, and hundreds died. Uprisings in the provinces were crushed, some 27,000 people were arrested, and thousands were deported to Algeria and Guiana. Victor Hugo tried to organize resistance and fled to Brussels, where in 1852 he wrote the pamphlet "Napoléon le Petit," and then to Jersey and Guernsey. In the plebiscite of December 20–21, about 7.4 million voted "yes" against 640,000 "no." A year later, on December 2, 1852, the president became Emperor Napoleon III. His support was both genuine — especially among peasants — and won through fear and censorship.
level.coup_1851.goal: A president barred from a second term dissolves the Assembly, hands the people universal suffrage — and millions approve the coup, while Hugo goes into exile
level.coup_1851.hint: Bayonets take Paris, but legitimacy comes from the ballot box. You could respect the constitution — but then there'd be no story.
level.coup_1851.intro: 1851. Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, president of the Second Republic and nephew of the emperor, was elected in 1848 by a huge majority. The constitution forbids him a second term, and the conservative Assembly has refused to amend it — and in 1850 it also curtailed universal suffrage, stripping some three million poor men of the vote. His half-brother, the Duke de Morny, is preparing an operation code-named "Rubicon."
level.coup_1851.source: Victor Hugo, 'Napoléon le Petit' (1852) and 'Histoire d'un crime' (1877); Karl Marx, 'Der achtzehnte Brumaire des Louis Bonaparte' (1852)
level.coup_1851.title: December 2
level.dreyfus_1898.fact: The handwriting only vaguely resembled Dreyfus's, but the court, after receiving a secret dossier, convicted him in December 1894; in January 1895 he was publicly stripped of his epaulettes and sent to Devil's Island. The antisemitic press rejoiced. In 1896 the new head of intelligence, Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart, intercepted the "petit bleu" sent by the German military attaché to Major Ferdinand Esterhazy, compared Esterhazy's letters with the note — and saw the same handwriting. Picquart himself was transferred to Tunisia. In January 1898 a court-martial acquitted Esterhazy, and two days later, on January 13, Émile Zola published in the newspaper L'Aurore an open letter to the president, "J'accuse…!" Zola was convicted of libel and fled to England. The country split into Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards, and the rift ran through families. In 1898 it came out that Lieutenant Colonel Henry had forged one of the pieces of evidence. In 1899 Dreyfus was convicted again but pardoned, and only in 1906 did a court fully exonerate him. The Affair gave rise to the League of Human Rights and the law of 1905.
level.dreyfus_1898.goal: Innocent Captain Dreyfus is convicted for another man's treason, an intelligence officer finds the real author, and Zola hurls an accusation at the whole army
level.dreyfus_1898.hint: The truth is found by a man inside the army — if they don't get rid of him first. The writer accuses, relying on the one who knows.
level.dreyfus_1898.intro: 1894. In a wastebasket at the German embassy in Paris, French intelligence finds a note — a list of secret documents offered for sale. The General Staff hunts for a traitor among its own. Suspicion falls on an artillery captain, Alfred Dreyfus, an Alsatian and a Jew.
level.dreyfus_1898.source: Émile Zola, 'J'accuse…!' (L'Aurore, January 13, 1898); Alfred Dreyfus, 'Cinq années de ma vie' (1901)
level.dreyfus_1898.title: The Dreyfus Affair
level.eleanor_1152.fact: As early as 1143, Bernard of Clairvaux, the most influential monk of the age, reminded the king during a dispute that he himself was married to a kinswoman. On March 21, 1152, a council of bishops at Beaugency declared the marriage void on grounds of consanguinity; the daughters remained legitimate and stayed with their father, while Aquitaine stayed with Eleanor. On the road to Poitiers, Count Theobald of Blois and Geoffrey, Henry of Anjou's younger brother, each tried to waylay her and force her into marriage — she slipped away. On May 18, 1152, Eleanor married Henry, who was eleven years her junior. In 1154 he became King Henry II of England, and his lands in France turned out larger than those of the French king himself. This is not the story of a love triangle: at stake were an inheritance, feudal rights and a balance of power that would lead to the wars between the Capetians and the Plantagenets.
level.eleanor_1152.goal: The marriage of Louis VII and Eleanor is annulled for consanguinity — and two months later she marries Henry of Anjou, taking Aquitaine with her
level.eleanor_1152.hint: The divorce begins with the king's doubt. A free duchess is a tempting prize: on the road to her groom, not only friends lie in wait.
level.eleanor_1152.intro: 1152. Fifteen years ago Eleanor, heiress to the vast Duchy of Aquitaine, married King Louis VII of France. Together they went on the Second Crusade, and there they quarreled for good. Their marriage has produced only two daughters. The king is pious and indecisive; the queen is clever, proud, and in full view of the whole court.
level.eleanor_1152.source: John of Salisbury, 'Historia Pontificalis'; Gervase of Canterbury, 'Chronica'
level.eleanor_1152.title: The Aquitaine Divorce
level.encyclopedie_1751.fact: D'Alembert's preface arranged all knowledge into a "tree" of memory, reason and imagination, in which theology became just one branch and the crafts stood equal to the sciences. In 1752 the King's Council banned the first two volumes. The head of royal censorship — the Directorate of the Book Trade — was Chrétien-Guillaume de Lamoignon de Malesherbes, a supporter of press freedom. According to a well-known story, he warned Diderot of a search and offered to hide the manuscripts in his own house. In 1759 the privilege was revoked and the pope condemned the Encyclopédie; d'Alembert had already left in 1758. Diderot carried on almost alone and in 1765 brought out the last ten volumes of articles disguised as a Swiss edition; the volumes of plates kept appearing until 1772. Already in 1764 he discovered that Le Breton had been secretly cutting the boldest passages from the proofs — and was furious. In all, 28 volumes and over 70,000 articles. The Encyclopédie was not a program for revolution, but it taught readers to ask of any custom: is it reasonable?
level.encyclopedie_1751.goal: The King's Council bans the Encyclopédie, France's chief censor hides its manuscripts in his own house — and Diderot sees the work through to the end
level.encyclopedie_1751.hint: Dangerous papers are hidden with someone nobody would search. Whoever quits the work won't finish printing it. And don't leave the publisher alone with the proofs.
level.encyclopedie_1751.intro: 1751. The publisher Le Breton planned to translate an English dictionary, and instead got Denis Diderot's life's work: the 'Encyclopédie, ou Dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers.' The co-editor is the mathematician Jean d'Alembert. The first volume comes out with a royal privilege, but the Jesuits and Jansenists are already hunting it for heresy.
level.encyclopedie_1751.source: 'Encyclopédie' (1751–1772), d'Alembert's 'Discours préliminaire'; Robert Darnton, 'The Business of Enlightenment' (1979)
level.encyclopedie_1751.title: The Encyclopédie Under Censorship
level.february_1848.fact: Guizot banned a large banquet set for February 22, and crowds poured into the streets. On February 23 the king dismissed Guizot, but that evening, outside the ministry on the Boulevard des Capucines, soldiers opened fire on the crowd and dozens died. The bodies were paraded through the city on carts, and barricades sprang up overnight. On February 24 Louis-Philippe abdicated in favor of his nine-year-old grandson, the Count of Paris, and fled to England. His daughter-in-law, the Duchess of Orléans, came to the Chamber with her son to ask for a regency — but a crowd burst in. The poet Alphonse de Lamartine and other deputies went to the Hôtel de Ville and proclaimed the republic. Lamartine persuaded the crowd to keep the tricolor rather than the red flag: "The tricolor has gone around the world." The Provisional Government introduced universal male suffrage — at Ledru-Rollin's insistence — abolished the death penalty for political crimes, and opened national workshops for the unemployed. Four months later, in June, their closure would spark a workers' uprising that the army would crush, leaving thousands dead.
level.february_1848.goal: A banned banquet turns into barricades, Louis-Philippe abdicates — and the poet Lamartine proclaims the Second Republic
level.february_1848.hint: The revolution starts at a table laid for speeches. A regency for a child has been offered before — don't give in. The republic's flag stays tricolor.
level.february_1848.intro: 1847–1848. Bad harvests, crisis, unemployment. Only about 250,000 wealthy men out of 35 million inhabitants can vote in France. Since political meetings are banned, the opposition holds "banquets" — dinners with speeches on electoral reform. Prime Minister François Guizot refuses to give ground.
level.february_1848.source: Alphonse de Lamartine, 'Histoire de la révolution de 1848' (1849); Alexis de Tocqueville, 'Souvenirs' (publ. 1893)
level.february_1848.title: February: A Republic in the Square
level.ferry_1882.fact: The Ferry laws built the school system step by step. The Camille Sée law of December 21, 1880, opened state lycées and collèges for girls. The law of June 16, 1881, made primary school free. The law of March 28, 1882, made it compulsory for children aged 6 to 13 and secular: religious instruction was replaced by "moral and civic education," and Thursday was left free so parents could take their children to catechism. The Catholic hierarchy, including Bishop Charles-Émile Freppel of Angers, protested fiercely. Every village gained a republican schoolteacher, and these teachers were dubbed the "black hussars of the Republic." There was a price, too: school taught only in French, and children who spoke Breton or Occitan in class were punished.
level.ferry_1882.goal: Jules Ferry makes primary school free, compulsory and secular, and Camille Sée opens state lycées for girls
level.ferry_1882.hint: Free first, then compulsory. The bishop will ask to keep the catechism in the classroom — that's the fork in the road.
level.ferry_1882.intro: 1880. The Third Republic is still unsure of itself: the monarchists are strong, and village schools are often run by nuns and religious brothers who teach the catechism above all. The Minister of Public Instruction Jules Ferry and the physiologist Paul Bert believe the republic needs citizens — and citizens are made in school.
level.ferry_1882.source: Laws of December 21, 1880, June 16, 1881, and March 28, 1882; Jules Ferry, 'Lettre aux instituteurs' (November 17, 1883)
level.ferry_1882.title: Ferry's School
level.gaillard_1204.fact: The siege began in August 1203. John's night attempt to relieve the castle by land and by river, led by William Marshal, failed, and in December John himself sailed off to England. The commander, Roger de Lacy, held out until spring and drove the civilians out of the castle — the enemy would not let them through, and many starved to death between the walls and the camp. On March 6, 1204, according to William the Breton, the French got into the castle through a chapel window, and the last ward fell. In the summer Pierre de Préaux, commander of Rouen, negotiated a thirty-day truce and sent to John for help; the king replied that he could not help. On June 24, 1204, Rouen surrendered. This was not a war of "France against England" but a quarrel between a king and a defiant vassal — yet after it the English kings were left on the continent with only the lands of Aquitaine south of Poitou, above all Gascony, while the Channel Islands remain under the British Crown to this day.
level.gaillard_1204.goal: Philip Augustus takes the impregnable Château Gaillard, John refuses to relieve Rouen — and Normandy passes to the French crown
level.gaillard_1204.hint: The key to Normandy is the castle above the Seine. An honest commander surrenders the city only with his lord's permission.
level.gaillard_1204.intro: 1203. Above the Seine stands Château Gaillard — a fortress that Richard the Lionheart built in just two years and called his "beautiful daughter." It guards the road to Rouen, the capital of Normandy. Richard is dead, and his brother John Lackland has become duke. King Philip II Augustus of France has declared that John, as a vassal, has forfeited his French fiefs — and has come to take them.
level.gaillard_1204.source: William the Breton, 'Philippide'; Rigord, 'Gesta Philippi Augusti'
level.gaillard_1204.title: Château Gaillard
level.gergovia_52bc.fact: Caesar himself recounts how Litaviccus led ten thousand Aedui toward Gergovia and on the way announced that the Romans had slaughtered their nobles. Caesar managed to intercept the column and show them the "murdered" men alive, but the Aeduan elite had already wavered, and Litaviccus went over to Vercingetorix. At Gergovia Caesar only meant to seize an advantageous hill, but the legionaries got carried away and climbed the walls, failing to hear the signal to retreat. The Gauls counterattacked: nearly seven hundred soldiers and forty-six centurions fell. Caesar lifted the siege, and soon the Aedui openly joined the rebels. This was Caesar's only major defeat at the hands of Vercingetorix. A few months later the war would be decided at Alesia. The Gauls were not a single nation but an alliance of tribes with their own calculations, and "France against Rome" has nothing to do with it.
level.gergovia_52bc.goal: Vercingetorix holds the heights of Gergovia, the Aedui break away from Rome — and Caesar suffers one of his heaviest defeats in Gaul
level.gergovia_52bc.hint: The legions are stronger in open field — fight where the ground is high. The Aedui are wavering, and whoever reaches them first will win them.
level.gergovia_52bc.intro: Spring of 52 BC. Gaul has risen against Caesar, led by the young Arvernian chieftain Vercingetorix. Caesar is besieging his home town of Gergovia on a high plateau. The Romans need their Aeduan allies — their grain and their cavalry. But the Aedui are divided: their chief magistrate Convictolitavis and the young nobleman Litaviccus are thinking of going over to the rebels.
level.gergovia_52bc.source: Gaius Julius Caesar, 'Commentarii de Bello Gallico', VII, 34–53
level.gergovia_52bc.title: Gergovia: A Victory Before Alesia
level.haiti_1804.fact: The rebels fought for freedom themselves. Sonthonax, who had no army, needed their sabers: in August 1793 he declared the slaves of the North free, and on February 4, 1794, the Convention abolished slavery in all the colonies. Toussaint went over to the Republic, drove out the Spanish and the British, and in 1801 issued a constitution making himself governor for life. Bonaparte sent an expedition under General Leclerc. In June 1802 Toussaint was invited to talks with General Brunet, arrested and shipped to France — he died in the Fort de Joux in April 1803. News that slavery had been restored on Guadeloupe set the island ablaze again. Jean-Jacques Dessalines took command of the war; the French army was destroyed by fighting and yellow fever, and Leclerc himself died. His successor Rochambeau waged war with extreme cruelty. On November 18, 1803, Dessalines's army took the fortifications of Vertières, and Rochambeau capitulated. On January 1, 1804, at Gonaïves, Dessalines proclaimed independence and gave the island back its Taíno name — Haiti. It is the only victorious revolution of enslaved people in history. In 1825, under threat from its fleet, France forced Haiti to pay 150 million francs in "compensation" to the former planters.
level.haiti_1804.goal: The rebel slaves of Saint-Domingue win the abolition of slavery, survive Toussaint's arrest and Bonaparte's expedition — and create Haiti
level.haiti_1804.hint: Freedom is proclaimed by whoever needs soldiers. When the leader is taken away, his heir will lead the war — unless he lays down his arms first.
level.haiti_1804.intro: 1791, Saint-Domingue — the richest colony in the world: sugar and coffee, half a million enslaved Africans and some forty thousand whites. In August a slave uprising erupts in the North. Toussaint, a former slave, coachman and healer, later known as Louverture, becomes one of its commanders. The Republic's commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax arrives in the ravaged colony, which the Spanish and British are already advancing on.
level.haiti_1804.source: Haitian Declaration of Independence (January 1, 1804); C. L. R. James, 'The Black Jacobins' (1938); Laurent Dubois, 'Avengers of the New World' (2004)
level.haiti_1804.title: Freedom Is Not a Gift
level.haussmann_1853.fact: In June 1853 Georges-Eugène Haussmann became prefect of the Seine department. Over seventeen years he cut straight boulevards through the old city, tore down tens of thousands of old houses and raised districts of uniform buildings in pale stone, and laid out the Bois de Boulogne, the Bois de Vincennes and public squares. The engineer Eugène Belgrand brought water into Paris from distant springs by aqueduct and built hundreds of kilometers of sewers — a city where cholera regularly broke out became healthier. But the rebuilding had another side: rents rose, working families were pushed out to the outskirts, and wide streets suit troops better than barricades. Haussmann borrowed money bypassing parliament. In 1868 a young lawyer, Jules Ferry, published the pamphlet "Les Comptes fantastiques d'Haussmann" — a pun on the "Contes d'Hoffmann." In January 1870 the prefect was dismissed, but we still see his Paris today.
level.haussmann_1853.goal: Napoleon III makes Haussmann prefect — and over seventeen years he reshapes Paris: boulevards, water, sewers, emptied neighborhoods
level.haussmann_1853.hint: Only someone given power can tear Paris apart. Nobody has checked Haussmann's accounts yet — don't rush the exposé.
level.haussmann_1853.intro: 1853. Paris is a cramped medieval city: crooked alleys where barricades go up, cholera, water drawn from the Seine. Emperor Napoleon III, who spent years in London, dreams of a new capital — with wide streets, parks and clean water. He needs a man who will fear neither landlords nor debts.
level.haussmann_1853.source: Georges-Eugène Haussmann, 'Mémoires' (1890–1893); Jules Ferry, 'Les Comptes fantastiques d'Haussmann' (1868)
level.haussmann_1853.title: Haussmann's Paris
level.jacquerie_1358.fact: On May 28, 1358, at Saint-Leu-d'Esserent, peasants killed several noblemen, and the revolt quickly engulfed the Beauvaisis and the surrounding lands: castles were burned, lords and their families killed. Guillaume Cale was chosen as leader and tried to turn the mobs into an army. Étienne Marcel sent a detachment of Parisians to help — on June 9, together with the peasants, they attacked the market at Meaux, where noble ladies had taken refuge, and were routed by knights. Charles of Navarre, seeking the nobles' support, invited Cale to a parley near Mello, seized him and crushed the now leaderless army. Cale was executed; according to one chronicle, before his execution he was "crowned" with a red-hot iron tripod. Reprisals followed in which thousands of peasants died, and Étienne Marcel was killed in Paris on July 31. Nearly everything we know was written down by the chroniclers Jean le Bel and Jean Froissart, who wrote for the nobility: they describe the rebels' atrocities in detail, the knights' revenge only briefly.
level.jacquerie_1358.goal: The peasants of the Beauvaisis rise against the nobles, but Charles of Navarre seizes their leader Guillaume Cale at a parley — and the revolt is drowned in blood
level.jacquerie_1358.hint: First the revolt gets a leader, the knights a commander. In open battle the knights are stronger, and a cautious leader won't go to a parley.
level.jacquerie_1358.intro: May 1358. King John II is a prisoner in England after the disaster at Poitiers, mercenary companies are plundering the land, and the lords demand new money from the peasants for ransoms. The nobles contemptuously call the peasant "Jacques Bonhomme." In Paris the Provost of the Merchants, Étienne Marcel, is fighting the Dauphin for power, and King Charles of Navarre, called the Bad, has his own eye on the French throne.
level.jacquerie_1358.source: Jean le Bel, 'Vrayes Chroniques'; Jean Froissart, 'Chroniques'; 'Chronique des quatre premiers Valois'
level.jacquerie_1358.title: The Jacquerie
level.july_1830.fact: On July 25 at Saint-Cloud the king signed four ordinances: freedom of the press was abolished, the newly elected Chamber dissolved, and the property qualification changed so that almost only large landowners could vote. Journalists, among them the young Adolphe Thiers, called for resistance. July 27–29 were the "Three Glorious Days": printers, workers and students built some four thousand barricades, some troops went over to the insurgents, and about 800 rebels and about 200 soldiers were killed. Charles X abdicated in favor of his grandson, but it was too late, and he left for exile in England. Republicans wanted a republic; bankers and liberal deputies wanted a new king. On July 31 the 72-year-old Lafayette embraced Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, on the balcony of the Paris Hôtel de Ville beneath the tricolor. Louis-Philippe became "King of the French," not "King of France." The July Revolution did not produce a republic, but it echoed across Europe — from Belgian independence to the Polish uprising. It lives on in Delacroix's painting "Liberty Leading the People."
level.july_1830.goal: Charles X's ordinances drive Paris to the barricades, the king flees — and instead of a republic, Lafayette gives France a "citizen king"
level.july_1830.hint: The king starts the revolution, not the street. Winning on the barricades doesn't decide who sits on the throne. A republic now would frighten those who pay.
level.july_1830.intro: July 1830. Charles X, brother of the executed Louis XVI, dreams of an old-regime monarchy. The elections have once again given the liberals a majority. Prime Minister Prince Jules de Polignac insists that the Virgin Mary advises him not to give way.
level.july_1830.source: Ordinances of Saint-Cloud (July 25, 1830); Charter of 1830; Eugène Delacroix, 'La Liberté guidant le peuple' (1830)
level.july_1830.title: Three Glorious Days
level.laicite_1905.fact: The Combes government closed thousands of schools run by religious congregations, and in 1904, after a quarrel over President Loubet's visit to Rome and the appointment of bishops, recalled its ambassador from the Vatican. Combes's bill would have kept the Church under state supervision, but in January 1905 his cabinet fell over a scandal about spying on Catholic officers. The socialist Aristide Briand became the law's rapporteur. He sought peace, not war: Article 4 handed church property to "associations of worshippers" organized according to the rules of their own church — and Jean Jaurès backed it. The law of December 9, 1905, guaranteed freedom of conscience and declared that the Republic neither recognizes, pays for, nor subsidizes any religion. Pope Pius X condemned the law in the encyclical Vehementer Nos, and the inventories of church property in 1906 sparked clashes at church doors. Laïcité is not a ban on religion but the neutrality of the state.
level.laicite_1905.goal: Combes breaks with the Vatican, Briand, backed by Jaurès, writes a compromise — and the Republic separates the churches from the state
level.laicite_1905.hint: Separation is possible once the old agreement is already torn up. A harsh bill will alienate those the law can't pass without.
level.laicite_1905.intro: 1904. For a hundred years France has been governed by Napoleon's Concordat: the state pays priests' salaries and the government appoints bishops. After the Dreyfus Affair, in which many Catholics stood against Dreyfus, republicans want to put an end to this. Prime Minister Émile Combes is a former seminarian and a fierce anticlerical.
level.laicite_1905.source: Law on the Separation of the Churches and the State of December 9, 1905; Pius X, encyclical 'Vehementer Nos' (1906)
level.laicite_1905.title: The Law of 1905
level.lyon_177.fact: We know of the persecution from a letter the Christians of Lyon themselves sent to "the brethren in Asia and Phrygia"; it was preserved by the church historian Eusebius. Bishop Pothinus died in prison after being beaten. Blandina, a frail slave, endured torture from morning till evening and repeated only: "I am a Christian, and nothing wicked is done among us." She was led into the amphitheater, tied to a stake, then thrown to a bull — she was the last to die. The governor consulted Emperor Marcus Aurelius, who replied: Roman citizens were to be beheaded, those who recanted set free. The presbyter Irenaeus had meanwhile been sent to Rome with a letter to Pope Eleutherius and survived. He became the next bishop of Lyon and wrote the famous treatise "Against Heresies." The persecution was local, not empire-wide, but its memory became one of the foundations of Christianity in Gaul. The number of dead — about fifty — is known only approximately.
level.lyon_177.goal: The slave Blandina does not recant under interrogation, and the presbyter Irenaeus carries away the account of the persecution — and all Christians learn of Lyon
level.lyon_177.hint: The witness must stay alive and free: whoever ends up under interrogation is no longer a messenger. The emperor's rescript won't settle the matter.
level.lyon_177.intro: AD 177, Lugdunum — today's Lyon, capital of Roman Gaul. The small Christian community, mostly Greeks from Asia Minor, is accused of "cannibalism" and "incest." A mob attacks the Christians, and the provincial governor throws them into prison and holds interrogations. Among those arrested are the ninety-year-old Bishop Pothinus and the slave Blandina.
level.lyon_177.source: 'Letter of the Churches of Vienne and Lyon' in: Eusebius of Caesarea, 'Ecclesiastical History', V, 1–4
level.lyon_177.title: The Martyrs of Lyon
level.mansurah_1250.fact: On February 8, 1250, the king's brother Robert of Artois, without waiting for the main force, charged into Mansourah and died in its narrow streets along with his knights. The sick army began to retreat, and on April 6 at Fariskur Louis was taken prisoner. In Damietta, three days after giving birth to a son, Margaret persuaded the Pisan and Genoese merchants not to abandon the city by promising to feed them at the crown's expense: Damietta became the main price of the king's freedom. The king was released in return for the city and a ransom of 400,000 livres, half of which was paid. On May 2 the Mamluks killed Turanshah and seized power in Egypt themselves. All of this was recounted by Jean de Joinville, seneschal of Champagne, who shared the king's captivity. Louis was canonized in 1297 as a model of piety and justice; yet he also waged crusades, and in 1242, on his orders, thousands of Talmud manuscripts were publicly burned in Paris. He died in 1270 outside Tunis, on a new crusade.
level.mansurah_1250.goal: The Seventh Crusade ends with Louis IX in captivity — and Queen Margaret holds Damietta, the price the king will pay for his freedom
level.mansurah_1250.hint: You can't ransom a dead king. To have something to pay with, someone must hold the city — and not flee from it.
level.mansurah_1250.intro: 1250, Egypt. Louis IX is leading a crusade against Cairo: a year ago the crusaders took the port of Damietta, and Queen Margaret of Provence stayed there, expecting a child. The army stands before the town of Mansourah, its camp ravaged by dysentery and scurvy. Egypt is ruled by the young Sultan Turanshah, while his army is in the grip of the Mamluk guards.
level.mansurah_1250.source: Jean de Joinville, 'Livre des saintes paroles et des bons faiz nostre saint roy Looÿs' (1309)
level.mansurah_1250.title: The King in Captivity
level.marne_1914.fact: Joffre retreated without losing control: he removed dozens of generals from their posts and shifted troops by rail. Von Kluck's German First Army, pursuing its enemy, swung east of Paris and exposed its flank. Gallieni saw it, and on September 5 Maunoury's army struck from the Ourcq River. On September 6 the whole line went over to the offensive; Ferdinand Foch's Ninth Army held out through heavy fighting at the Marshes of Saint-Gond — the famous "My center is giving way, my right is retreating — excellent, I attack" is more likely a legend. The British and French pushed into the gap between the German armies, and on September 9 the German command ordered a retreat to the Aisne. Moltke the Younger was soon replaced. Some six hundred Paris taxis really did carry several thousand soldiers to the front, but maneuver and railways decided the outcome. There was no quick war: the front dug into trenches for four years.
level.marne_1914.goal: Having retreated almost to Paris, Joffre keeps his army intact, Gallieni strikes the open flank — and the Germans fall back from the Marne
level.marne_1914.hint: First survive, then find the flank. The taxis are a legend, not the key to victory.
level.marne_1914.intro: August 1914. Under the Schlieffen Plan the German armies are outflanking the French through Belgium and are meant to take Paris in six weeks. French attacks in Lorraine have collapsed with enormous losses, and the commander-in-chief Joseph Joffre is pulling his armies south. The government leaves for Bordeaux; the old general Joseph Gallieni stays behind to defend the capital.
level.marne_1914.title: The Miracle of the Marne
level.massalia_600bc.fact: The legend, retold by the Roman historian Justin, says that Gyptis passed by all the neighbors and held out the cup to the stranger Protis. Her father decided the gods had guided her choice, accepted the Greek as his son-in-law and gave him land by the sea, at the Bay of Lacydon. There Massalia grew up — today's Marseille. In Aristotle, as retold by Athenaeus, it is the same story, only the bride is called Petta and the groom Euxenus. The founding of Massalia by the Phocaeans is a historical fact confirmed by archaeology, while the wedding tale is a legend explaining the Greeks' friendship with their neighbors. The Gauls, moreover, were not the "first Frenchmen," and Massalia remained a Greek city for centuries.
level.massalia_600bc.goal: A Greek seafarer comes as a guest to a wedding feast, the princess offers the cup to him — and Massalia rises on the shore
level.massalia_600bc.hint: The cup is offered to a guest, not a conqueror. The neighbor suitor at the feast is waiting too — don't rush the bride's choice.
level.massalia_600bc.intro: Around 600 BC. Greek ships from Phocaea put in at the mouth of the Rhône. Their leader Protis goes to Nannus, king of the local Segobriges tribe, to ask for friendship. And the king happens to be holding a feast: by custom his daughter Gyptis will choose her own husband — offering a cup of water to the man she favors. Noble Gallic suitors sit at the table.
level.massalia_600bc.source: Justin, 'Epitome of the Philippic History of Pompeius Trogus', XLIII, 3; Athenaeus, 'Deipnosophistae', XIII (after Aristotle)
level.massalia_600bc.title: Gyptis Chooses the Cup
level.melusine.fact: The legend tells that Melusine was the daughter of a Scottish king and the fairy Pressine, and as punishment for wronging her father, every Saturday she became a serpent below the waist. Married to Raymondin, she built castles overnight — Lusignan, Parthenay, Vouvant — and bore ten sons, nearly every one with a marvelous birthmark; two became kings of Cyprus and Armenia. But Raymondin's brother, the Count of Forez, whispered to him that on Saturdays his wife met a lover. Raymondin pierced the door with his sword and saw his wife in her bath with a serpent's tail. At first he kept silent, but later, in anger, he publicly called her a "serpent" — and Melusine flew out of the window as a winged serpent. Ever since, it was said, she shrieks over the towers of Lusignan before the death of each lord of the castle. Jean d'Arras wrote down the romance for the Duke of Berry: the Lusignans who ruled Cyprus traced their line to the fairy.
level.melusine.goal: A fairy makes a knight swear never to seek her on Saturdays, builds him the castle of Lusignan and bears him sons who become kings
level.melusine.hint: Their happiness hangs on a single oath. Whoever whispers about Saturdays is no friend of this house.
level.melusine.intro: Poitou, long ago. While hunting, the young knight Raymondin accidentally killed his uncle the count and rides through the forest in despair. At the Spring of Thirst he meets three beautiful ladies. The eldest, Melusine, knows of his misfortune and offers salvation: she will become his wife and bring him lands and glory. There is one condition — on Saturdays he must never see her or look for her.
level.melusine.source: Jean d'Arras, 'Roman de Mélusine' (1393); Coudrette, 'Roman de Mélusine' (c. 1401)
level.melusine.title: Melusine
level.mutinies_1917.fact: On April 16, 1917, the offensive began and failed: the Germans knew about it, the artillery had not cut the wire, and losses in the first days exceeded a hundred thousand men. From late April, "collective refusals" broke out in dozens of divisions: soldiers agreed to hold the trenches but refused to go into new attacks, sang the "Internationale," and demanded leave and peace. On May 15 War Minister Paul Painlevé replaced Nivelle with Pétain. Pétain visited some ninety divisions, introduced regular leave, improved food and rest, and announced he would wait for "the Americans and the tanks." There were punishments: courts-martial handed down over three thousand sentences, some 550 of them death sentences, but according to the historian Guy Pedroncini, only about fifty men were actually shot. The Germans never found out about the mutinies. The mutineers of 1917 were neither cowards nor revolutionaries: they refused to die for nothing.
level.mutinies_1917.goal: After Nivelle's offensive fails, soldiers refuse to go into pointless attacks — and Pétain calms the army with leave, food and rest
level.mutinies_1917.hint: The soldiers will hold the front, but they won't go into the meat grinder. A new commander is needed to listen, not to shoot indiscriminately.
level.mutinies_1917.intro: April 1917. General Robert Nivelle, hero of Verdun, promises that a single mighty blow on the Chemin des Dames ridge will break the front within forty-eight hours. The poilus — as French soldiers are called — are in their third year in the trenches, there is almost no leave, and behind the lines there are rumors of revolution in Russia.
level.mutinies_1917.title: The Mutinies of 1917
level.nantes_1598.fact: In March 1598 Mercœur submitted. In April, at Nantes, the king signed the edict: 92 general articles, secret articles, and two royal warrants, the "brevets." The Huguenots received freedom of conscience, the right to worship in specified places, access to public office and mixed law courts, as well as some hundred and fifty fortified places of refuge garrisoned at the king's expense. Catholicism was restored everywhere it had been banned. This was not modern religious freedom but a compromise among people weary of war. The Parlement of Paris, led by its First President Achille de Harlay, resisted for almost a year; in February 1599 the king summoned its members and said: "I am king, and I speak to you as king" — and the edict was registered. Henry IV was murdered in 1610 by the fanatic Ravaillac, and his grandson Louis XIV revoked the edict in 1685.
level.nantes_1598.goal: Having forced the last leader of the League to submit, Henry IV signs the Edict of toleration at Nantes — and makes the Parlement accept it
level.nantes_1598.hint: Peace with the Protestants is possible once the war with the League is over. Promise exactly as much as the Catholics will stomach — or the Parlement will dig in its heels.
level.nantes_1598.intro: 1598. Thirty-six years of religious wars. The former Huguenot leader Henry of Navarre has become King Henry IV and, to enter Paris, converted to Catholicism himself. The last to hold out against him is the Duke of Mercœur, leader of the Catholic League in Brittany. The Huguenots fear a Catholic king will forget them and demand guarantees; their voice is Philippe Duplessis-Mornay, known as the "Huguenot pope."
level.nantes_1598.source: Edict of Nantes (April 1598); speech of Henry IV to the Parlement of Paris (February 1599)
level.nantes_1598.title: The Edict of Nantes
level.paris_1763.fact: France's Caribbean islands, with sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans, brought the treasury more than all of New France. Voltaire, in "Candide," had already called Canada "a few acres of snow." Under the Treaty of Paris of February 10, 1763, France ceded Canada and Louisiana east of the Mississippi to Britain, but got back Guadeloupe and Martinique, along with fishing rights off Newfoundland and the islets of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. Even earlier, in 1762, Louis XV had secretly given New Orleans and western Louisiana to his ally Spain. France's Native allies on the Great Lakes learned from the British themselves that their lands had been "handed over" to the British. In 1763 the Ottawa chief Pontiac and his allies took eight British forts and besieged Detroit and Fort Pitt. Pontiac hoped the French would return, but no help came. The war led the British Crown, in the Royal Proclamation of 1763, to forbid settlers from moving beyond the Appalachians — which would later become one of the American colonists' grievances.
level.paris_1763.goal: Having lost the Seven Years' War, France trades Canada for the sugar islands — and the peoples of the Great Lakes, who were never asked, rise against their new masters
level.paris_1763.hint: Sugar is worth more to France than snow. Cabinets sign the peace, but the land belongs to those never invited to the table — and they have no reason to wait for the French.
level.paris_1763.intro: 1762. The Seven Years' War is lost: the British have taken Quebec and Montreal, Guadeloupe and Martinique. Louis XV's minister, the Duke de Choiseul, is negotiating with the British prime minister Lord Bute. Not everything can be recovered — a choice must be made.
level.paris_1763.source: Treaty of Paris (February 10, 1763); Royal Proclamation of 1763; Richard White, 'The Middle Ground' (1991)
level.paris_1763.title: Sugar or Snow
level.pepin_751.fact: In 750 Pepin sent Bishop Burchard and Abbot Fulrad to Pope Zachary with a question: was it good that in the land of the Franks the kings had no power? The pope replied that it was better to call king the one who held the power, so that order would not be disturbed. In 751 at Soissons the Franks elected Pepin king, and Childeric III was tonsured and sent to the monastery of Saint-Bertin — long hair was the dynasty's symbol. Pepin was anointed by the bishops; later chronicles name Boniface as the one who anointed him, but historians are not sure of this. In 754 Pope Stephen II himself anointed Pepin and his sons. Thus the Church consecrated the power of the Carolingian dynasty. The image of the Merovingian "do-nothing kings" was largely created by Carolingian writers who needed to justify the coup.
level.pepin_751.goal: Mayor of the Palace Pepin asks the pope who deserves the crown, has the last Merovingian shorn as a monk — and becomes an anointed king
level.pepin_751.hint: The crown is taken not with a sword but with a question. First Rome, then the shears, then the holy oil.
level.pepin_751.intro: The mid-8th century. Officially the kings of the Franks are still the descendants of Clovis — the Merovingians. But all power is held by the mayors of the palace, the "stewards of the court," from the family of Charles Martel. Charles's son Pepin commands the army and the treasury, while King Childeric III, in the words of a contemporary, merely sits on the throne with his long hair — the mark of royal blood.
level.pepin_751.source: 'Annales regni Francorum' for 749–751; Einhard, 'Vita Karoli Magni', ch. 1
level.pepin_751.title: Pepin Changes the Dynasty
level.revocation_1685.fact: Dragoons were billeted in Protestant homes: the soldiers ate, drank, beat and ruined their hosts until they signed an abjuration. The intendants sent Versailles lists of tens of thousands of "new converts," and the king came to believe that hardly any Protestants were left. On October 18, 1685, he signed the Edict of Fontainebleau: the Edict of Nantes was revoked, Protestant churches were demolished, pastors had to leave within 15 days, and lay people were forbidden to leave on pain of the galleys. Even so, 150,000 to 200,000 Huguenots fled — to Holland, England, Prussia and Switzerland — taking their crafts and capital with them. Those who remained met in secret, in the "Desert." The lawyer Claude Brousson became a preacher at these gatherings; in 1698 he was captured and broken on the wheel at Montpellier. In March of that same year, 1685, the "Code Noir" was issued — a law on slavery in the French islands: it legalized masters' power over enslaved people and required them to be baptized Catholic. Toleration for Protestants returned only with the edict of 1787.
level.revocation_1685.goal: Having "converted" the Protestants with dragoons, Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes — and two hundred thousand Huguenots secretly flee France
level.revocation_1685.hint: The king needs lists, and the lists need dragoons. The banished pastor will still be useful — if he doesn't recant.
level.revocation_1685.intro: The 1680s. "One king, one law, one faith" — Louis XIV wants to bring back to Catholicism the million French Protestants, the Huguenots, whom the Edict of Nantes of 1598 allowed to worship. They are stripped of offices and paid to convert, and the war minister, the Marquis de Louvois, finds a more reliable method.
level.revocation_1685.source: Edict of Fontainebleau (October 18, 1685); 'Code Noir' (March 1685); Élie Benoist, 'Histoire de l'édit de Nantes' (1693–1695)
level.revocation_1685.title: The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
level.rights_1789.fact: Lafayette discussed his draft with the American envoy Thomas Jefferson. Between August 20 and 26 the Assembly adopted the 17 articles of the "Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen": "Men are born and remain free and equal in rights," sovereignty resides in the nation, law is the expression of the general will, freedom of speech, the presumption of innocence, property as "an inviolable and sacred right." Louis XVI dragged his feet on approving it. Mounier fought for an absolute royal veto and a two-chamber parliament, but lost: the king got only a suspensive veto. A banquet of the Flanders Regiment's officers at Versailles, where tricolor cockades were rumored to have been trampled, set hungry Paris alight: on October 5 thousands of women marched on Versailles, followed by Lafayette's National Guard. The king approved the Declaration and on October 6 moved to Paris. But the Declaration had its limits: the rights of citizens were not extended to women — in 1791 Olympe de Gouges would answer with the "Declaration of the Rights of Woman" — nor to the poor below the property qualification, nor to enslaved people in the colonies.
level.rights_1789.goal: The Assembly proclaims that men are born free and equal in rights — and it takes the market women of Paris to make the king approve the Declaration
level.rights_1789.hint: First the Declaration is written, then it's voted on. The king stalls on signing — it's the street, not the deputies, that can convince him. Better not advise him to take an absolute veto.
level.rights_1789.intro: August 1789. The Bastille has fallen, and on the night of August 4 the deputies abolished the privileges of the estates. Now the Constituent Assembly wants to write down what the new France will stand on. General Lafayette, a veteran of the American war, brings a draft. The monarchist Jean-Joseph Mounier wants a strong king; Abbé Sieyès wants power for the nation.
level.rights_1789.source: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (August 26, 1789); Olympe de Gouges, 'Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne' (1791)
level.rights_1789.title: The Rights of Man — and Their Limits
level.rocroi_1643.fact: The Duke of Enghien kept the news of the king's death secret from the army. He knew that General Beck's corps was marching to join Melo, and decided to attack without waiting for it. At dawn on May 19, Enghien's French cavalry routed the Spanish left wing and swept round into the rear. The Spanish infantry — the famous tercios, considered among the best foot soldiers in Europe — stood in square under the fire of French cannon; their aged commander, the Count of Fontaine, was killed. After several attacks were beaten off, the remnants of the tercios surrendered. The Spanish lost about 7,000 killed and thousands taken prisoner. Rocroi did not break Spain at once — the war went on until 1659 — but it became a symbol of a new balance of power in Europe. And in Paris, power under the little king passed to the regent Anne of Austria and Cardinal Mazarin. The victor of Rocroi would become the "Great Condé" — and in 1650–1651 one of the leaders of the Fronde of the Princes.
level.rocroi_1643.goal: The king is dead, a child is on the throne, and the twenty-one-year-old Duke of Enghien hurls himself at the invincible Spanish tercios — and breaks them
level.rocroi_1643.hint: The soldiers don't need to hear bad news. While you deliberate, reinforcements are marching to the enemy. A square can't be broken head-on — first strip it of its cavalry.
level.rocroi_1643.intro: May 1643. Francisco de Melo's Spanish army is besieging the fortress of Rocroi in the Ardennes — the road to Paris is almost open. On May 14 Louis XIII dies; King Louis XIV is four years old. Marching to meet the Spanish is an army under the twenty-one-year-old Louis de Bourbon, Duke of Enghien — with the experienced Marshal L'Hôpital assigned to restrain him from recklessness.
level.rocroi_1643.source: Henri d'Orléans, Duke of Aumale, 'Histoire des princes de Condé pendant les XVIe et XVIIe siècles' (1863–1896)
level.rocroi_1643.title: Rocroi
level.roland_778.fact: The "Song of Roland" tells how Ganelon secretly sold Roland to Marsile, and in the pass of Roncevaux a huge army fell upon the rearguard. Three times Oliver begged him to sound the horn Oliphant, but Roland refused — he would not shame himself and sweet France. When almost all had fallen, he blew it at last, so hard that his temples burst. Ganelon assured Charles that Roland was just out hunting, but the emperor turned back, routed the Saracens and executed the traitor — he was torn apart by four horses. In reality, on August 15, 778, in the Roncevaux Pass, the Frankish rearguard, in which "Hruodland, prefect of the Breton March" fell, was wiped out by Basque mountaineers, not Saracens. The epic, written down around 1100 in the age of the Crusades, turned a border skirmish into a holy war of Christians against Muslims.
level.roland_778.goal: Ganelon betrays the rearguard to Marsile, Roland sounds the horn at the last moment — and Charlemagne returns for revenge
level.roland_778.hint: The betrayal happens in Zaragoza, not at Roncevaux. Pride is a poor counselor, and the man who'll say "he's just hunting" must not stand beside the emperor.
level.roland_778.intro: 778. Charlemagne is returning from a campaign in Spain. His envoy Count Ganelon went to the Saracen king Marsile in Zaragoza to negotiate peace. Ganelon hates his stepson, the valiant Roland: it was Roland who proposed sending him on the dangerous embassy. The army is withdrawing over the Pyrenees, with Roland, his friend Oliver and the twelve peers in the rearguard.
level.roland_778.source: 'La Chanson de Roland' (poem, c. 1100; Oxford manuscript, 12th century); Einhard, 'Vita Karoli Magni', ch. 9
level.roland_778.title: Roland Sounds the Horn
level.rollo_911.fact: In the summer of 911 Rollo besieged Chartres, but Margrave Robert and Duke Richard of Burgundy defeated him beneath its walls; according to tradition, the bishop carried a relic — the tunic of the Virgin — onto the ramparts. After the defeat, Archbishop Franco of Rouen talked Rollo into making peace. At Saint-Clair-sur-Epte the king gave him lands on the lower Seine, and Rollo promised to be baptized and to defend the river against other Vikings; in 912 he was baptized under the name Robert, with Margrave Robert as his godfather. The text of the treaty has not survived, and almost everything we know comes from the chronicle of Dudo of Saint-Quentin, written a century later. Dudo also tells how Rollo refused to kiss the king's foot, and one of his warriors lifted the royal foot to his mouth instead — and the king toppled over backwards. The lands of the "Northmen" became Normandy, and Rollo's descendant William would conquer England in 1066.
level.rollo_911.goal: Defeated at Chartres, the Viking chief Rollo agrees to be baptized and receives lands on the lower Seine from the king
level.rollo_911.hint: No one sues for peace who hasn't lost yet. And don't let the Viking go off raiding again — nobody will make a deal with a plunderer.
level.rollo_911.intro: 911. For almost a hundred years the Northmen have sailed up the Seine, burning monasteries and extorting ransom from Paris. Their chief Rollo has settled in Rouen. The King of the West Franks, Charles III, called the Simple, cannot drive them out by force — and his vassal, Margrave Robert of Neustria, defends his lands on his own.
level.rollo_911.source: Dudo of Saint-Quentin, 'De moribus et actis primorum Normanniae ducum' (c. 1015)
level.rollo_911.title: Rollo Gets Normandy
level.schoelcher_1848.fact: Schœlcher headed the commission and insisted on immediate abolition, without the "preparatory" period the planters demanded. On April 27, 1848, the government signed the decree: slavery was abolished in all colonies two months after the decree was proclaimed there. But the enslaved did not wait. On Martinique, after the arrest of a slave named Romain, thousands rose up on May 22 in Saint-Pierre and the surrounding area; people were killed, and on May 23 the governor himself proclaimed abolition without waiting for the ship from Paris; on May 27 the same happened on Guadeloupe. The new citizens got the vote: on Guadeloupe a former slave, the carpenter Louisy Mathieu, was elected deputy. The Martinican Cyrille Bissette, himself once deported for a pamphlet against slavery, competed with Schœlcher for votes. A law of 1849 paid compensation for the "loss of property" — to the former owners, not to the formerly enslaved. May 22 is celebrated on Martinique as Abolition Day.
level.schoelcher_1848.goal: Schœlcher wins immediate abolition of slavery, the rebels of Martinique seize freedom without waiting for the ship, and a former slave becomes a deputy
level.schoelcher_1848.hint: A job half done means ten more years of slavery. On the islands, freedom isn't waited for — it's taken. And the money for the "loss" goes to anyone but those who suffered.
level.schoelcher_1848.intro: March 1848. The Second Republic has just been born. Slavery, abolished by the Convention in 1794, was restored by Bonaparte in 1802, and some 250,000 people live in bondage on Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana and Réunion. Victor Schœlcher, a Parisian from an Alsatian family, who has written against slavery for twenty years, becomes undersecretary to François Arago, Minister of the Navy and the Colonies.
level.schoelcher_1848.source: Decree abolishing slavery (April 27, 1848); Victor Schœlcher, 'Des colonies françaises. Abolition immédiate de l'esclavage' (1842)
level.schoelcher_1848.title: The Second Decree of Freedom
level.sedan_1870.fact: On July 13, 1870, King Wilhelm I telegraphed from the spa town of Ems about his conversation with the French ambassador. Bismarck cut the text so that it sounded like an insult and gave it to the newspapers. On July 19 France declared war — formally the aggressor. The German armies under Moltke the Elder moved faster: one French army was bottled up in Metz, and the second, Marshal MacMahon's army, accompanied by the ailing Napoleon III, was surrounded at the fortress of Sedan. On September 1 MacMahon was wounded at the very start of the battle, an attempt to break out failed, and on September 2 the emperor surrendered along with some hundred thousand soldiers. On September 4 a crowd burst into the Palais Bourbon, and Léon Gambetta proclaimed the republic at the Hôtel de Ville. The war went on: Paris endured a siege, and Gambetta flew out of it by balloon to raise new armies. On January 18, 1871, the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, and under the peace France gave up Alsace and part of Lorraine.
level.sedan_1870.goal: Bismarck provokes a war, Moltke encircles an army at Sedan, the emperor surrenders — and two days later Paris proclaims a republic
level.sedan_1870.hint: The war is started not by a cannon but by a telegram. The republic won't be proclaimed while the emperor is on his throne rather than in captivity.
level.sedan_1870.intro: July 1870. The France of the Second Empire trusts its army and fears a rising Prussia. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck wants war: it will unite the German states around Berlin. All he needs is a pretext — and a dispute over a candidate for the Spanish throne supplies it.
level.sedan_1870.source: Otto von Bismarck, 'Gedanken und Erinnerungen' (1898); Émile Zola, 'La Débâcle' (1892)
level.sedan_1870.title: Sedan
level.soissons_vase.fact: The story is told by Gregory of Tours. Clovis asked his army to give him the vase over and above his share, and almost everyone agreed. Only one warrior struck it with his axe: "You shall have nothing here but what the lot gives you." The king bore it and handed the fragments to the bishop's messenger. A year later, at the March review, he went up to that warrior, declared that his weapons were the worst kept of all, and threw his axe to the ground — and when the man bent down, split his skull, saying: "Thus you did to the vase at Soissons." Gregory concludes that by this he inspired great fear in everyone. It is an instructive tale about how a war-band leader became a king, not a record of the event; Gregory was writing almost a hundred years later.
level.soissons_vase.goal: A warrior smashes the vase the king promised to the bishop — and Clovis waits a year to take revenge before the whole army
level.soissons_vase.hint: The king needs not the vase but fear. Revenge in public at the review is law; a blow struck in anger is mere murder.
level.soissons_vase.intro: 486. The young Frankish king Clovis has just defeated the last Roman ruler of Gaul and is dividing the spoils at Soissons. Among the trophies is a precious vase from a church. Bishop Remigius asks for it back. But the Franks divide plunder by lot, and in this the king is just one warrior among many.
level.soissons_vase.title: The Vase of Soissons
level.syagrius_486.fact: According to Gregory of Tours, Clovis defeated Syagrius, who fled to Toulouse, to Alaric II, King of the Visigoths. Clovis demanded that the fugitive be handed over, threatening war. Alaric took fright and surrendered Syagrius in chains; Clovis kept him under guard and later had him secretly killed. Thus the Franks gained northern Gaul with Paris and Soissons. Even earlier, Bishop Remigius of Reims had written Clovis a letter: the young pagan king should respect the bishops and heed their advice — the alliance of the Franks with the Gallo-Roman Church began long before the baptism. The "fall of Rome" in Gaul was gradual: the Franks were one of several post-Roman powers, alongside the Visigoths, Burgundians and Bretons.
level.syagrius_486.goal: Clovis defeats Syagrius, ruler of the last Roman fragment of Gaul, and forces the Visigoths to hand him over
level.syagrius_486.hint: The Roman won't share — he has to be defeated. And only the one who sheltered the fugitive can hand him over.
level.syagrius_486.intro: 486. The Western Roman Empire has been gone for ten years, but in northern Gaul, around Soissons, a Roman domain still holds out. It is ruled by Syagrius — the Franks call him "King of the Romans." The twenty-year-old king of the Salian Franks, Clovis, challenges him to battle.
level.syagrius_486.source: Gregory of Tours, 'Historia Francorum', II, 27; letter of Remigius to Clovis ('Epistolae Austrasicae', 2)
level.syagrius_486.title: Soissons: The Last Roman of Gaul
level.tonkin_1885.fact: Ferry waged the war piecemeal, without a declaration, begging small credits from the Chamber. Admiral Amédée Courbet's squadron destroyed the Chinese fleet at Fuzhou in 1884. In March 1885 a panicked dispatch reached Paris about a retreat from Lạng Sơn. Clemenceau declared that he no longer wished to debate with the ministers, only to judge them — on March 30 the cabinet fell, and Ferry was dubbed "the Tonkinese." Peace with China was signed in June, and Tonkin stayed French. In July 1885, in a speech on the colonies, Ferry said that the "higher races" had a right and a duty to civilize the "lower" ones; Clemenceau replied that this was the right of the strong dressed up in words about civilization. And in Vietnam in July 1885, Regent Tôn Thất Thuyết attacked the French at Huế, took the young Emperor Hàm Nghi into the mountains and issued the Cần Vương edict — "Aid the King." The resistance lasted more than ten years.
level.tonkin_1885.goal: Jules Ferry leads France into Indochina — his cabinet falls over a dispatch from Lạng Sơn, and in Vietnam the "Aid the King" movement rises
level.tonkin_1885.hint: The one who falls is the one who started the war first. A grand speech about colonies won't help the premier here.
level.tonkin_1885.intro: 1883. Prime Minister Jules Ferry — the same man who created the secular school — is convinced that without colonies France will become a second-rate power. He sends troops and a fleet to Tonkin, in northern Vietnam, where the Nguyễn empire recognizes the authority of the Chinese emperor. Opposing him is the radical Georges Clemenceau: money and soldiers are needed at home, against Germany.
level.tonkin_1885.source: Speech by Jules Ferry in the Chamber of Deputies on July 28, 1885, and Georges Clemenceau's reply on July 30 ('Journal officiel', 1885)
level.tonkin_1885.title: Ferry the Tonkinese
level.tours_732.fact: Beaten, Odo acknowledged Charles's seniority, and Charles led the Franks south. In October 732 (or, by some accounts, 733), between Tours and Poitiers, the Franks formed a dense wall of infantry and waited for a week. The Spanish Chronicle of 754 writes: "the men of the North stood like a wall, motionless as ice." Abd al-Rahman was killed, and during the night his army withdrew, abandoning its camp. Later Charles received the nickname Martel — "the Hammer." European historians of the 19th century called the battle the salvation of Christian Europe, but today it is more often seen as the repulse of a major raid: wars with the Umayyads in southern Gaul went on for decades more, and the victory helped Charles subdue Aquitaine and strengthen his own power.
