level.tours_732.goal: The Umayyad governor ravages Aquitaine, Duke Odo calls on the Franks for help — and Charles Martel stops the raid near Poitiers
level.tours_732.hint: The Franks will come only if they're called — and the one to call them is the one who has nothing left to lose. In open field the emir's cavalry is stronger.
level.tours_732.intro: 732. Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, governor of al-Andalus, crosses the Pyrenees with a large cavalry army. Duke Odo of Aquitaine is an old rival of the Franks: he even made an alliance with the Berber ruler Munuza. Now Abd al-Rahman crushes Odo on the Garonne and marches north toward the rich Abbey of Saint Martin at Tours. The only force able to stop him is the Franks of the mayor of the palace, Charles.
level.tours_732.title: Tours and Poitiers: Raid or Turning Point?
level.vassy_1562.fact: On January 17, 1562, the Edict of Saint-Germain allowed Huguenots to worship — but only outside city walls. On Sunday, March 1, Duke François de Guise and his retinue were passing through the small town of Wassy in Champagne, where several hundred Protestants were worshipping in a barn inside the town. A quarrel broke out, stones flew — and the duke's armed men burst into the barn: about fifty people were killed and more than a hundred wounded. The Protestants called it a massacre; Guise claimed he had been attacked first. Paris welcomed the duke as a hero, and on April 2 Prince Louis de Condé seized Orléans and called his fellow believers to arms. Thus began the first of eight wars of religion, which lasted until the Edict of Nantes in 1598; Guise himself was shot in 1563 by the Protestant Poltrot de Méré. Neither Catholics nor Protestants were monolithic: the rift ran through courts, towns and families.
level.vassy_1562.goal: The regent allows Protestants to worship, the Duke of Guise's retinue carries out a massacre at Wassy — and the Prince of Condé calls the Huguenots to arms
level.vassy_1562.hint: The massacre happens where worship has already been permitted — but not inside the town walls. It's too early for the Admiral to take the stage: his hour will come in 1572.
level.vassy_1562.intro: 1562. King Charles IX is eleven years old, and his mother Catherine de' Medici rules. There are already hundreds of thousands of Protestant Huguenots in France, among them princes of the blood and Admiral Coligny. The Catholic party is led by the mighty Duke François de Guise. Catherine seeks a compromise to keep the country out of war.
level.vassy_1562.source: 'Histoire ecclésiastique des Églises réformées au royaume de France' (1580); Jean Perrissin and Jacques Tortorel, engravings 'Quarante tableaux' (1570)
level.vassy_1562.title: Wassy
level.verdun_1916.fact: On February 21, 1916, some twelve hundred German guns opened fire, and four days later Fort Douaumont fell. The defense was entrusted to General Philippe Pétain. He organized supply along the single road from Bar-le-Duc — it was named the "Sacred Way," and trucks rolled along it without pause — and the rotation of divisions, the "noria": about three quarters of the French army passed through Verdun. His order ended with the words "Courage! We'll get them!", while "They shall not pass" is associated with General Robert Nivelle, who replaced Pétain in May. In May Charles Mangin's attack on Douaumont failed. Only on October 24 did a carefully prepared strike by Nivelle and Mangin retake the fort. The battle lasted until December: some 300,000 French and Germans were killed and hundreds of thousands wounded. Verdun became a shared memory of two nations — and a symbol of a senseless meat grinder.
level.verdun_1916.goal: Falkenhayn strikes at Verdun, Pétain holds the front by rotating divisions along the Sacred Way — and by autumn the French retake Fort Douaumont
level.verdun_1916.hint: The city is held not by a heroic attack but by a road and troop rotation. A hasty strike at the fort will only add to the dead.
level.verdun_1916.intro: February 1916. The chief of the German General Staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, chooses Verdun for his blow — a salient in the front that the French cannot abandon out of pride. He later wrote that he wanted to "bleed white" the French army; historians debate whether this was the plan from the start or invented after the fact.
level.verdun_1916.source: Philippe Pétain, 'La Bataille de Verdun' (1929); Alistair Horne, 'The Price of Glory: Verdun 1916' (1962)
level.verdun_1916.title: Verdun
level.verdun_843.fact: On June 25, 841, at Fontenoy near Auxerre, Louis and Charles defeated Lothair in a bloody battle. In February 842 at Strasbourg the brothers swore an alliance before their armies: Louis in the Romance tongue, understood by Charles's warriors, and Charles in the Teutonic tongue, understood by Louis's men. Nithard recorded both texts — the "Oaths of Strasbourg" are considered the oldest surviving document of the French language. In August 843 at Verdun the empire was divided: Charles the Bald received the western lands, Louis the German the eastern, and Lothair the imperial title and a long strip from the North Sea to Italy. The West Frankish kingdom became the core of future France and the East Frankish of Germany, but in 843 no one was yet thinking of these countries: it was a family division of an inheritance.
level.verdun_843.goal: Charlemagne's grandsons fight over his inheritance, the younger brothers swear to each other in two languages — and at Verdun the empire is split in three
level.verdun_843.hint: The eldest can't be beaten alone. The oath is sworn by the victors, and the division comes when everyone has something to divide.
level.verdun_843.intro: 840. Emperor Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, has died. His eldest son Lothair has received the imperial title and wants power over the whole empire. The younger sons — Louis, ruling beyond the Rhine, and Charles, son of the second marriage, ruling in the west — disagree. Their cousin Nithard, a warrior and historian, sees it all with his own eyes and writes it down.
level.verdun_843.source: Nithard, 'Historiarum libri IIII' (841–843), book III, ch. 5 — texts of the Oaths of Strasbourg; 'Annales Bertiniani' for 843
level.verdun_843.title: The Partition of Verdun
level.villers_1539.fact: In August 1539, at the Château of Villers-Cotterêts, the king signed an ordinance of 192 articles. Articles 110 and 111 required that all court decisions and legal acts be drawn up "in the French mother tongue and not otherwise." The main target was Latin; historians debate whether Breton or Occitan counted as a "mother tongue," but the ordinance did not forbid speaking them. Article 51 obliged parish priests to keep registers of baptisms with dates — the first regular birth records, which became the basis of civil registration. Chancellor Poyet himself fell from favor and was put on trial in 1542. The ordinance is the oldest law still in force in France, and since 2023 the Château of Villers-Cotterêts has housed the International City of the French Language.
level.villers_1539.goal: Francis I signs the ordinance at Villers-Cotterêts: the courts speak French, and curés record every baptism
level.villers_1539.hint: The law is written by the chancellor, not by the king himself. And this law was at war with Latin, not with the languages of the provinces.
level.villers_1539.intro: 1539. King Francis I, patron of Leonardo and builder of Chambord, wants to keep a firm grip on his kingdom: uniform courts, understandable laws. For now, verdicts and contracts are written in Latin, which many litigants don't understand, and finding out who was born when is nearly impossible — there are no records. Chancellor Guillaume Poyet is preparing a great ordinance on justice.
level.villers_1539.title: The King's French
